paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump said he could pardon Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang if it were ever needed, according to an interview with the New York Post that Investing.com summarized on November 24, 2026. Trump described a pardon as always an option, while adding that he did not think one would be necessary.

In the same conversation, Trump said it was probably not too late for the U.S. government to take an equity stake in Nvidia. He said he had thought about the idea but had not raised it so far, according to both Investing.com and a Firstpost report summarized by Inshorts.

The comments came days before Huang is scheduled to testify before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Banking Committee. Trump said Huang should tell the truth in those hearings and should not need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights, according to the Investing.com report.
Lawmakers are examining Huang over potential national security concerns and alleged violations of U.S. export controls on chip shipments to China, the report said.

As a precedent for a government stake, Trump pointed to the 10% stake the U.S. government took in Intel last year. Inshorts, citing Firstpost, noted that Trump personally owns Nvidia shares and that Nvidia is the second largest company in the world.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12, 2026, after admitting to an affair with a businesswoman whom U.S. authorities reportedly suspected of links to Chinese intelligence, a claim that IBTimes UK said had not been established as fact. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO at the time.

Trump intervened to secure Huang's reinstatement, arguing that the company's leadership was critical to U.S. leadership in AI, according to Investing.com. Al Jazeera reported that Nvidia's shares rose 31.5% on Monday, November 23, which it described as the largest single day gain in U.S. stock market history.

The rally did not last across the sector. Al Jazeera reported on November 25 that Asian chip stocks fell sharply, with Taiwan's Taiex down as much as 7.9% and South Korea's Kospi down more than 6%, after the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.5% on Tuesday.

The two remarks point in different directions for investors. A pardon discussion keeps the legal questions around Huang in the headlines just before he faces lawmakers, while talk of a federal stake raises the possibility that Washington could become a shareholder in one of the largest companies in the world, as it did with Intel. Neither step has been taken, and Trump framed both as options rather than plans.

Huang's testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Banking Committee next week is the next moment to watch, along with any concrete step by the administration toward a stake in Nvidia.
